text: Two teams can run the identical algorithm on the identical problem and get wildly different bills, purely because of which backend and pricing model they chose. This lesson works through real, current pricing so you can estimate cost before committing to an architecture, not after the invoice arrives.

We'll cover AWS Braket's real per-task and per-shot pricing across vendors, how IBM Quantum's runtime-second billing compares, how program sets cut cost for batched workloads, and why the cheapest backend isn't automatically the right choice.

Here's the same two-hundred-task, thousand-shot job priced on three real devices. IonQ Aria: six thousand sixty dollars. Rigetti Ankaa-3: two hundred forty dollars. OQC Lucy: one hundred thirty dollars. A twenty-five to forty-six times spread, for the identical workload, purely from which device you pick.

And here's the real control behind every one of those numbers — Amazon Braket's actual form for setting a per-device spending cap. This is where the abstract pricing table becomes a concrete, enforced ceiling.

Here's that cap once it's live — real per-QPU spending limits on the Braket console. This is the operational side of the pricing lesson: numbers you compute on paper only matter once they're enforced somewhere real.

Azure Quantum prices differently again — a marketplace model set per hardware partner. Here's Microsoft's own real diagram of their resource estimator, built around an entirely different estimation approach. Three real providers, three real pricing dimensions — which is exactly why picking the cheapest backend in isolation is a mistake. Connectivity, error rate, and queue depth all factor into whether a cheap device is actually the right choice.

Next lesson turns "how long will this take" into an actual number you can set and defend before a project starts — because Chapter 3 already showed the honest answer is almost entirely about queue depth.
